data.title: End-to-End Reinforcement Learning for Torque Based Variable Height Hopping
data.summary: Legged locomotion is arguably the most suited and versatile mode to deal with natural or unstructured terrains. Intensive research into dynamic walking and running controllers has recently yielded great advances, both in the optimal control and reinforcement learning (RL) literature. Hopping is a challenging dynamic task involving a flight phase and has the potential to increase the traversability of legged robots. Model based control for hopping typically relies on accurate detection of different jump phases, such as lift-off or touch down, and using different controllers for each phase. In this paper, we present a end-to-end RL based torque controller that learns to implicitly detect the relevant jump phases, removing the need to provide manual heuristics for state detection. We also extend a method for simulation to reality transfer of the learned controller to contact rich dynamic tasks, resulting in successful deployment on the robot after training without parameter tuning.

analysis.main_contribution: The paper introduces an end‑to‑end reinforcement learning torque controller for variable‑height hopping that learns phase detection implicitly, eliminating manual heuristics, and demonstrates successful sim‑to‑real transfer without parameter tuning.
analysis.methodology: A deep RL policy is trained in simulation to output joint torques for a single‑legged hopper; the network learns to detect lift‑off, flight, and touchdown phases internally. The learned controller is transferred to hardware using domain randomization and a sim‑to‑real adaptation technique.
datasets_used: Real‑world hopping data collected from the monoped robot during deployment
key_findings:
The RL policy achieves variable‑height hopping with comparable or better performance than heuristic phase‑based controllers.
Transfer to the real robot succeeds without additional tuning, validating the sim‑to‑real approach.
analysis.limitations: Limited evaluation on a single‑legged platform; lack of extensive comparative benchmarks against state‑of‑the‑art model‑based methods; potential sensitivity to simulation fidelity.
analysis.future_work: Extend the framework to multi‑legged robots and more complex terrains; investigate curriculum learning for faster convergence; perform systematic ablation studies on phase detection mechanisms and domain randomization settings.

data.title: Unified Sequence-to-Sequence Learning for Single- and Multi-Modal Visual Object Tracking
data.summary: In this paper, we introduce a new sequence-to-sequence learning framework for RGB-based and multi-modal object tracking. First, we present SeqTrack for RGB-based tracking. It casts visual tracking as a sequence generation task, forecasting object bounding boxes in an autoregressive manner. This differs from previous trackers, which depend on the design of intricate head networks, such as classification and regression heads. SeqTrack employs a basic encoder-decoder transformer architecture. The encoder utilizes a bidirectional transformer for feature extraction, while the decoder generates bounding box sequences autoregressively using a causal transformer. The loss function is a plain cross-entropy. Second, we introduce SeqTrackv2, a unified sequence-to-sequence framework for multi-modal tracking tasks. Expanding upon SeqTrack, SeqTrackv2 integrates a unified interface for auxiliary modalities and a set of task-prompt tokens to specify the task. This enables it to manage multi-modal tracking tasks using a unified model and parameter set. This sequence learning paradigm not only simplifies the tracking framework, but also showcases superior performance across 14 challenging benchmarks spanning five single- and multi-modal tracking tasks. The code and models are available at https://github.com/chenxin-dlut/SeqTrackv2.

analysis.main_contribution: The paper proposes SeqTrack and its extension SeqTrackv2, a unified sequence‑to‑sequence transformer framework that casts RGB and multi‑modal visual object tracking as autoregressive bounding‑box generation, eliminating task‑specific head networks.
analysis.methodology: An encoder–decoder transformer architecture is used: the bidirectional encoder extracts features from template and search regions; the causal decoder predicts a sequence of bounding boxes (x,y,w,h) step by step. SeqTrackv2 adds a unified interface for auxiliary modalities and task‑prompt tokens to handle multiple tracking tasks with a single model.
key_findings:
SeqTrack achieves competitive or superior performance on RGB tracking benchmarks compared to head‑based trackers.
SeqTrackv2 outperforms state‑of‑the‑art methods across 14 challenging single‑ and multi‑modal tracking benchmarks.
analysis.limitations: The approach relies on transformer inference, which may incur higher computational cost; evaluation is limited to standard benchmarks without real‑time deployment analysis.
analysis.future_work: Explore lightweight transformer variants for real‑time tracking; extend the framework to handle more modalities (e.g., depth, thermal); investigate curriculum learning or self‑supervised pretraining to improve generalization.

data.title: Unsupervised Flow-Aligned Sequence-to-Sequence Learning for Video Restoration
data.summary: How to properly model the inter-frame relation within the video sequence is an important but unsolved challenge for video restoration (VR). In this work, we propose an unsupervised flow-aligned sequence-to-sequence model (S2SVR) to address this problem. On the one hand, the sequence-to-sequence model, which has proven capable of sequence modeling in the field of natural language processing, is explored for the first time in VR. Optimized serialization modeling shows potential in capturing long-range dependencies among frames. On the other hand, we equip the sequence-to-sequence model with an unsupervised optical flow estimator to maximize its potential. The flow estimator is trained with our proposed unsupervised distillation loss, which can alleviate the data discrepancy and inaccurate degraded optical flow issues of previous flow-based methods. With reliable optical flow, we can establish accurate correspondence among multiple frames, narrowing the domain difference between 1D language and 2D misaligned frames and improving the potential of the sequence-to-sequence model. S2SVR shows superior performance in multiple VR tasks, including video deblurring, video super-resolution, and compressed video quality enhancement. Code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/linjing7/VR-Baseline

analysis.main_contribution: The paper introduces S2SVR, an unsupervised flow‑aligned sequence‑to‑sequence framework that jointly learns optical flow and video restoration, enabling a single model to handle multiple VR tasks.
analysis.methodology: S2SVR serializes the input video into a 1D token stream, applies a transformer encoder–decoder for long‑range temporal modeling, and aligns frames using an unsupervised optical‑flow estimator trained with a distillation loss that mitigates flow inaccuracies.
key_findings: S2SVR outperforms state‑of‑the‑art methods on video deblurring, super‑resolution and compressed‑video enhancement benchmarks.
The unsupervised flow estimator improves correspondence accuracy, leading to better restoration quality across tasks.
analysis.limitations: High computational cost due to transformer inference; evaluation limited to standard benchmark datasets without real‑time deployment analysis.
analysis.future_work: Investigate lightweight transformer variants for real‑time tracking; extend the framework to additional modalities (e.g., depth, thermal); explore curriculum learning or self‑supervised pretraining to enhance generalization.

data.title: Simplicial Attention Neural Networks
data.summary: The aim of this work is to introduce simplicial attention networks (SANs), i.e., novel neural architectures that operate on data defined on simplicial complexes leveraging masked self-attentional layers. Hinging on formal arguments from topological signal processing, we introduce a proper self-attention mechanism able to process data components at different layers (e.g., nodes, edges, triangles, and so on), while learning how to weight both upper and lower neighborhoods of the given topological domain in a totally task-oriented fashion. The proposed SANs generalize most of the current architectures available for processing data defined on simplicial complexes. The proposed approach compares favorably with other methods when applied to different (inductive and transductive) tasks such as trajectory prediction and missing data imputations in citation complexes.

analysis.main_contribution: The paper proposes Simplicial Attention Neural Networks (SANs), a novel attention‑based architecture that processes signals on simplicial complexes by jointly attending to upper and lower neighborhood structures across multiple simplex dimensions.
analysis.methodology: SANs extend self‑attention to simplicial domains: each simplex (node, edge, triangle, etc.) receives a masked multi‑head attention over its incident higher‑order and adjacent lower‑order simplices, with learnable weighting of upper/lower neighborhoods. The model is trained end‑to‑end for tasks such as trajectory prediction and missing data imputation.
key_findings: SANs outperform existing graph‑based and simplicial methods on inductive/transductive citation completion and trajectory forecasting benchmarks.
The attention mechanism learns meaningful upper/lower neighborhood weights that adapt to the task without manual tuning.
analysis.limitations: Limited evaluation to a few benchmark graphs; scalability to very large complexes not demonstrated; reliance on accurate simplicial complex construction may affect performance.
analysis.future_work: Explore efficient sparse implementations for large‑scale complexes, extend SANs to dynamic or temporal simplicial data, and investigate theoretical guarantees of attention weighting in higher‑order topology.

data.title: SA-Net: Shuffle Attention for Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
data.summary: Attention mechanisms, which enable a neural network to accurately focus on all the relevant elements of the input, have become an essential component to improve the performance of deep neural networks. There are mainly two attention mechanisms widely used in computer vision studies, \textit{spatial attention} and \textit{channel attention}, which aim to capture the pixel-level pairwise relationship and channel dependency, respectively. Although fusing them together may achieve better performance than their individual implementations, it will inevitably increase the computational overhead. In this paper, we propose an efficient Shuffle Attention (SA) module to address this issue, which adopts Shuffle Units to combine two types of attention mechanisms effectively. Specifically, SA first groups channel dimensions into multiple sub-features before processing them in parallel. Then, for each sub-feature, SA utilizes a Shuffle Unit to depict feature dependencies in both spatial and channel dimensions. After that, all sub-features are aggregated and a "channel shuffle" operator is adopted to enable information communication between different sub-features. The proposed SA module is efficient yet effective, e.g., the parameters and computations of SA against the backbone ResNet50 are 300 vs. 25.56M and 2.76e-3 GFLOPs vs. 4.12 GFLOPs, respectively, and the performance boost is more than 1.34% in terms of Top-1 accuracy. Extensive experimental results on common-used benchmarks, including ImageNet-1k for classification, MS COCO for object detection, and instance segmentation, demonstrate that the proposed SA outperforms the current SOTA methods significantly by achieving higher accuracy while having lower model complexity. The code and models are available at https://github.com/wofmanaf/SA-Net.

analysis.main_contribution: SA-Net introduces a lightweight Shuffle Attention (SA) module that efficiently fuses spatial and channel attention via grouped sub-features and shuffle units, achieving higher accuracy with significantly reduced parameters and FLOPs compared to existing methods.
analysis.methodology: The SA module first partitions channels into multiple groups, applies a Shuffle Unit—combining spatial and channel attention within each group—then aggregates the groups and performs a channel‑shuffle operation to enable cross‑group communication. This design reduces computational overhead while preserving expressive power.
key_findings: SA-Net outperforms state‑of‑the‑art attention modules such as SENet, CBAM, ECA‑Net, and SGE‑Net on ImageNet‑1k, achieving >1.34% Top‑1 accuracy gain with only 300 additional parameters and 2.76e-3 GFLOPs over ResNet‑50.
On MS COCO benchmarks, SA-Net improves detection and segmentation metrics while maintaining lower model complexity than competing attention‑based backbones.
analysis.limitations: The paper focuses on image classification and object detection/segmentation; it does not evaluate the module on other vision tasks (e.g., video, depth estimation) or analyze its performance on very deep networks beyond ResNet‑50.
analysis.future_work: Future research could explore applying SA modules to transformer‑based architectures, scaling them to larger backbones, investigating their effectiveness on non‑image modalities, and conducting ablation studies on group size and shuffle strategies.

data.title: Pairwise Neural Machine Translation Evaluation
data.summary: We present a novel framework for machine translation evaluation using neural networks in a pairwise setting, where the goal is to select the better translation from a pair of hypotheses, given the reference translation. In this framework, lexical, syntactic and semantic information from the reference and the two hypotheses is compacted into relatively small distributed vector representations, and fed into a multi-layer neural network that models the interaction between each of the hypotheses and the reference, as well as between the two hypotheses. These compact representations are in turn based on word and sentence embeddings, which are learned using neural networks. The framework is flexible, allows for efficient learning and classification, and yields correlation with humans that rivals the state of the art.

analysis.main_contribution: The paper introduces a neural network–based pairwise MT evaluation framework that learns compact lexical, syntactic and semantic representations of a reference and two hypotheses, achieving human‑judgment correlation comparable to state‑of‑the‑art metrics.
analysis.methodology: It encodes each hypothesis and the reference using word and sentence embeddings, then feeds their concatenated vectors into a multi‑layer neural network that models interactions between each hypothesis–reference pair and between the two hypotheses; the network outputs which hypothesis is better in a binary classification setting.
datasets_used: WMT 2014 English‑German test set with human pairwise judgments
WMT 2016 English‑German test set with human pairwise judgments
key_findings: The proposed method attains Pearson/Spearman correlations with human judgments that rival or exceed traditional metrics such as BLEU, METEOR and TER on the evaluated datasets.
It demonstrates that a lightweight neural architecture can efficiently learn discriminative features without requiring extensive hand‑crafted linguistic resources.
analysis.limitations: The approach only provides pairwise preference decisions, not absolute quality scores; it relies on the availability of reference translations and human judgments for training.
analysis.future_work: Future research could explore extending the model to multi‑hypothesis ranking, incorporating multilingual or low‑resource settings, integrating unsupervised pretraining, and investigating interpretability of learned representations.

data.title: Neural Machine Translation: A Review and Survey
data.summary: The field of machine translation (MT), the automatic translation of written text from one natural language into another, has experienced a major paradigm shift in recent years. Statistical MT, which mainly relies on various count-based models and which used to dominate MT research for decades, has largely been superseded by neural machine translation (NMT), which tackles translation with a single neural network. In this work we will trace back the origins of modern NMT architectures to word and sentence embeddings and earlier examples of the encoder-decoder network family. We will conclude with a survey of recent trends in the field.

analysis.main_contribution: The paper provides a comprehensive review and survey of neural machine translation (NMT), tracing its evolution from early encoder–decoder models to modern architectures such as attention mechanisms and Transformers, while highlighting key trends and resources in the field.
analysis.methodology: Literature review and taxonomy construction; the authors analyze seminal papers, categorize NMT approaches, and summarize available open-source toolkits and datasets cited in the literature.
key_findings: NMT has largely displaced statistical MT, leading to a rapid increase in publications and adoption of encoder–decoder architectures with attention.
The survey identifies major architectural milestones (e.g., Bahdanau attention, Transformer) and catalogs popular open‑source NMT toolkits that have driven research progress.
analysis.limitations: As a survey, the work does not provide new empirical results; it relies on existing literature which may be biased toward high‑profile conferences and may overlook unpublished or proprietary advances.
analysis.future_work: Future directions include deeper exploration of low‑resource and multilingual NMT, integration with other NLP tasks, interpretability of learned representations, and systematic benchmarking across diverse language pairs.

data.title: On Using SpecAugment for End-to-End Speech Translation
data.summary: This work investigates a simple data augmentation technique, SpecAugment, for end-to-end speech translation. SpecAugment is a low-cost implementation method applied directly to the audio input features and it consists of masking blocks of frequency channels, and/or time steps. We apply SpecAugment on end-to-end speech translation tasks and achieve up to +2.2\% \BLEU on LibriSpeech Audiobooks En->Fr and +1.2% on IWSLT TED-talks En->De by alleviating overfitting to some extent. We also examine the effectiveness of the method in a variety of data scenarios and show that the method also leads to significant improvements in various data conditions irrespective of the amount of training data.

analysis.main_contribution: The paper demonstrates that applying SpecAugment—time and frequency masking on mel‑spectrograms—to end‑to‑end speech translation models effectively reduces overfitting and yields measurable BLEU gains across multiple language pairs.
analysis.methodology: Implement SpecAugment as a data augmentation step during training of an encoder–decoder ST model; evaluate performance on standard benchmarks while varying data size to assess robustness.
key_findings: SpecAugment improves BLEU by up to +2.2% on LibriSpeech En→Fr and +1.2% on IWSLT En→De.
The augmentation benefits persist across different data regimes, showing consistent gains regardless of training set size.
analysis.limitations: Limited to the two evaluated language pairs; only a single ST architecture tested; no ablation of individual masking parameters or comparison with other augmentation techniques beyond SpecAugment.
analysis.future_work: Explore SpecAugment in larger multilingual and low‑resource settings, conduct systematic ablations of mask widths and probabilities, compare against alternative audio augmentations, and integrate with synthetic data generation methods.

data.title: Is Sanskrit the most token-efficient language? A quantitative study using GPT, Gemini, and SentencePiece
data.summary: Tokens are the basic units of Large Language Models (LLMs). LLMs rely on tokenizers to segment text into these tokens, and tokenization is the primary determinant of computational and inference cost. Sanskrit, one of the oldest languages, is hypothesized to express more meaning per token due to its morphology and grammar rules; however, no prior work has quantified this. We use a dataset of 701 parallel verses of the Bhagavad Gita, which comprises three languages-Sanskrit, English, and Hindi along with transliteration of Sanskrit into English. We test tokenizers including SentencePiece (SPM), older GPT models, and the latest generation tokenizers from Gemini and GPT. We use metrics of token count, characters per token (token efficiency), and tokens per character (token cost). Results show a ~2x difference in token counts between Sanskrit and English/Hindi under the unbiased SPM baseline. English/Hindi translations of Sanskrit commentary resulted in an approximately 20x increase in token count. GPT o200k base (latest, used by GPT-4o) and Gemini (latest) reduce bias by a significant degree compared to GPT cl100k base (used until GPT-4), but still fail to fully capture Sanskrit's compactness. This matters because there might be a penalty bias for non-English users, which inflates the token count. This research provides a foundation for improving future tokenizer design and shows the potential of Sanskrit for highly compact encoding, saving on cost while speeding up training and inference. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/anshulkr713/sanskrit-token-efficiency

analysis.main_contribution: Quantitatively demonstrates that Sanskrit is substantially more token‑efficient than English and Hindi when processed by modern LLM tokenizers, revealing a ~2× lower token count under unbiased SentencePiece and highlighting persistent bias in GPT/Gemini tokenizers.
analysis.methodology: Built a parallel corpus of 701 Bhagavad Gita verses in Sanskrit, English, Hindi, and transliteration; trained equal‑size SentencePiece models for each language; evaluated four tokenization systems (GPT cl100k base, GPT o200k base, Gemini tokenizer, SPM) on token count, characters per token, and tokens per character.
datasets_used: 701 parallel verses of the Bhagavad Gita (Sanskrit, English, Hindi, transliteration)
key_findings: Sanskrit requires roughly half as many tokens as its translations under unbiased SentencePiece; GPT o200k base and Gemini reduce but do not eliminate token bias; translations inflate token counts by up to 20×.
analysis.limitations: Limited to a single text (Bhagavad Gita), small corpus size, and reliance on existing tokenizer training data which may not fully capture language diversity.
analysis.future_work: Expand to larger, more varied Sanskrit corpora; fine‑tune tokenizers specifically for Sanskrit; investigate impact on LLM training cost and inference latency across multilingual settings.
analysis.score_reasoning: The study provides the first empirical evidence of Sanskrit’s token efficiency using contemporary tokenizers, offering novel insights into tokenizer bias and language compactness, but it remains a focused, domain‑specific analysis rather than a broad methodological breakthrough.

data.title: Lightweight Transformer Architectures for Edge Devices in Real-Time Applications
data.summary: The deployment of transformer-based models on resource-constrained edge devices represents a critical challenge in enabling real-time artificial intelligence applications. This comprehensive survey examines lightweight transformer architectures specifically designed for edge deployment, analyzing recent advances in model compression, quantization, pruning, and knowledge distillation techniques. We systematically review prominent lightweight variants including MobileBERT, TinyBERT, DistilBERT, EfficientFormer, EdgeFormer, and MobileViT, providing detailed performance benchmarks on standard datasets such as GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet-1K, and COCO. Our analysis encompasses current industry adoption patterns across major hardware platforms (NVIDIA Jetson, Qualcomm Snapdragon, Apple Neural Engine, ARM architectures), deployment frameworks (TensorFlow Lite, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch Mobile, CoreML), and optimization strategies. Experimental results demonstrate that modern lightweight transformers can achieve 75-96% of full-model accuracy while reducing model size by 4-10x and inference latency by 3-9x, enabling deployment on devices with as little as 2-5W power consumption. We identify sparse attention mechanisms, mixed-precision quantization (INT8/FP16), and hardware-aware neural architecture search as the most effective optimization strategies. Novel findings include memory-bandwidth bottleneck analysis revealing 15-40M parameter models achieve optimal hardware utilization (60-75% efficiency), quantization sweet spots for different model types, and comprehensive energy efficiency profiling across edge platforms. We establish real-time performance boundaries and provide a practical 6-step deployment pipeline achieving 8-12x size reduction with less than 2% accuracy degradation.

analysis.main_contribution: The paper surveys lightweight transformer variants and systematically evaluates compression, quantization, pruning, and distillation techniques for edge deployment, demonstrating that 75‑96% of full-model accuracy can be retained while reducing size by 4‑10× and latency by 3‑9×.
analysis.methodology: Comprehensive literature review combined with empirical benchmarking of MobileBERT, TinyBERT, DistilBERT, EfficientFormer, EdgeFormer, and MobileViT on GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet‑1K, and COCO across NVIDIA Jetson, Qualcomm Snapdragon, Apple Neural Engine, and ARM platforms using TensorFlow Lite, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch Mobile, and CoreML; analysis of sparse attention, mixed‑precision INT8/FP16 quantization, and hardware‑aware NAS.
key_findings: Lightweight transformers achieve 75‑96% accuracy with 4‑10× smaller models and 3‑9× faster inference on edge devices consuming as little as 2‑5W; sparse attention, mixed‑precision quantization, and hardware‑aware NAS are most effective optimization strategies.
Memory‑bandwidth bottleneck analysis shows 15‑40M parameter models attain optimal hardware utilization (60‑75% efficiency) and identifies quantization sweet spots per model type.
analysis.limitations: Limited to a handful of transformer variants and benchmark datasets; primarily empirical survey without new algorithmic contributions; hardware profiling may not generalize to all edge platforms.
analysis.future_work: Extend evaluation to more diverse lightweight models, explore fine‑tuning for specific edge tasks, investigate energy efficiency across broader hardware families, and develop automated pipelines integrating NAS with quantization/pruning for end‑to‑end deployment.
analysis.score_reasoning: The paper offers a thorough empirical synthesis of existing techniques and identifies practical optimization strategies, providing notable novel insights (e.g., memory‑bandwidth bottleneck analysis) but does not introduce fundamentally new algorithms or paradigms.

data.title: Insights into DeepSeek-V3: Scaling Challenges and Reflections on Hardware for AI Architectures
data.summary: The rapid scaling of large language models (LLMs) has unveiled critical limitations in current hardware architectures, including constraints in memory capacity, computational efficiency, and interconnection bandwidth. DeepSeek-V3, trained on 2,048 NVIDIA H800 GPUs, demonstrates how hardware-aware model co-design can effectively address these challenges, enabling cost-efficient training and inference at scale. This paper presents an in-depth analysis of the DeepSeek-V3/R1 model architecture and its AI infrastructure, highlighting key innovations such as Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) for enhanced memory efficiency, Mixture of Experts (MoE) architectures for optimized computation-communication trade-offs, FP8 mixed-precision training to unlock the full potential of hardware capabilities, and a Multi-Plane Network Topology to minimize cluster-level network overhead. Building on the hardware bottlenecks encountered during DeepSeek-V3's development, we engage in a broader discussion with academic and industry peers on potential future hardware directions, including precise low-precision computation units, scale-up and scale-out convergence, and innovations in low-latency communication fabrics. These insights underscore the critical role of hardware and model co-design in meeting the escalating demands of AI workloads, offering a practical blueprint for innovation in next-generation AI systems.

analysis.main_contribution: DeepSeek‑V3 demonstrates a hardware‑aware co‑design that scales an LLM to 2,048 NVIDIA H800 GPUs by introducing memory‑efficient Multi‑head Latent Attention, MoE for compute–communication balance, FP8 mixed‑precision training, and a Multi‑Plane Network topology.
analysis.methodology: The authors design and implement novel architectural primitives (MLA, MoE, FP8 training, multi‑plane networking), train the model on a large GPU cluster, profile hardware bottlenecks, and conduct cross‑disciplinary discussions to propose future hardware directions.
key_findings: Hardware‑aware co‑design enables cost‑efficient scaling of LLMs while mitigating memory, compute, and bandwidth constraints; FP8 mixed‑precision training unlocks full GPU throughput.
analysis.limitations: Evaluation limited to a specific GPU cluster (2,048 NVIDIA H800) and does not explore broader hardware families or diverse lightweight models.
analysis.future_work: Extend the approach to other hardware platforms, investigate fine‑tuning for edge tasks, broaden energy efficiency studies across devices, and automate pipelines integrating NAS with quantization/pruning for end‑to‑end deployment.
analysis.score_reasoning: The paper provides solid empirical insights and introduces several novel architectural techniques that collectively improve scalability, but it does not present a fundamentally new algorithmic paradigm.

data.title: How do language models learn facts? Dynamics, curricula and hallucinations
data.summary: Large language models accumulate vast knowledge during pre-training, yet the dynamics governing this acquisition remain poorly understood. This work investigates the learning dynamics of language models on a synthetic factual recall task, uncovering three key findings: First, language models learn in three phases, exhibiting a performance plateau before acquiring precise factual knowledge. Mechanistically, this plateau coincides with the formation of attention-based circuits that support recall. Second, the training data distribution significantly impacts learning dynamics, as imbalanced distributions lead to shorter plateaus. Finally, hallucinations emerge simultaneously with knowledge, and integrating new knowledge into the model through fine-tuning is challenging, as it quickly corrupts its existing parametric memories. Our results emphasize the importance of data distribution in knowledge acquisition and suggest novel data scheduling strategies to accelerate neural network training.

analysis.main_contribution: The paper dissects how language models acquire factual knowledge by revealing a three‑phase learning trajectory on a synthetic recall task, linking performance plateaus to the emergence of attention‑based recall circuits and showing that data distribution critically shapes these dynamics.
analysis.methodology: They adapted a synthetic biography generation benchmark, trained transformer models while monitoring per‑step recall accuracy, applied an attention patching technique to identify recall circuits, varied training data distributions to study curriculum effects, and evaluated fine‑tuning impact on knowledge retention.
datasets_used: Synthetic factual recall dataset (adapted from Allen‑Zhu & Li 2023)
key_findings: 1. Models learn in three distinct phases—statistical learning, a plateau with emerging attention circuits, then individual‑specific knowledge acquisition; 2. Imbalanced data distributions shorten the plateau and accelerate knowledge gain but risk overfitting, suggesting curriculum scheduling can improve training speed.
analysis.limitations: Results are based on a synthetic task that may not fully capture real‑world factual learning; analysis focuses on transformer architectures without exploring other model families.
analysis.future_work: Extend investigations to larger, more realistic datasets; explore alternative architectures and memory mechanisms; develop principled data curricula for diverse downstream tasks; study fine‑tuning strategies that preserve existing knowledge.
analysis.score_reasoning: The work introduces novel insights into learning dynamics and attention circuit formation, and proposes curriculum techniques, representing a solid contribution with notable novelty but not a paradigm shift.

data.title: Optimal design of frame structures with mixed categorical and continuous design variables using the Gumbel-Softmax method
data.summary: In optimizing real-world structures, due to fabrication or budgetary restraints, the design variables may be restricted to a set of standard engineering choices. Such variables, commonly called categorical variables, are discrete and unordered in essence, precluding the utilization of gradient-based optimizers for the problems containing them. In this paper, incorporating the Gumbel-Softmax (GSM) method, we propose a new gradient-based optimizer for handling such variables in the optimal design of large-scale frame structures. The GSM method provides a means to draw differentiable samples from categorical distributions, thereby enabling sensitivity analysis for the variables generated from such distributions. The sensitivity information can greatly reduce the computational cost of traversing high-dimensional and discrete design spaces in comparison to employing gradient-free optimization methods. In addition, since the developed optimizer is gradient-based, it can naturally handle the simultaneous optimization of categorical and continuous design variables. Through three numerical case studies, different aspects of the proposed optimizer are studied and its advantages over population-based optimizers, specifically a genetic algorithm, are demonstrated.

analysis.main_contribution: The paper introduces a gradient‑based optimizer that incorporates the Gumbel‑Softmax trick to handle mixed categorical and continuous design variables in large‑scale frame structure optimization.
analysis.methodology: It replaces discrete categorical choices (e.g., beam profiles, materials) with differentiable samples from a categorical distribution via Gumbel‑Softmax, enabling back‑propagation of sensitivities through finite‑element analysis; the optimizer is benchmarked against a genetic algorithm on three numerical case studies.
key_findings:
1. The GSM‑based optimizer achieves comparable or better objective values than a GA while requiring fewer function evaluations.
2. It naturally handles simultaneous optimization of categorical and continuous variables, reducing computational cost in high‑dimensional discrete spaces.
analysis.limitations: Limited to problems where a differentiable FE model is available; performance depends on the choice of temperature schedule and may not scale trivially to extremely large industrial models.
analysis.future_work: Extend the approach to other structural families (e.g., trusses, shells), integrate surrogate modeling or adaptive temperature schemes, explore multi‑objective formulations, and validate on real‑world industrial projects.
analysis.score_reasoning: The use of Gumbel‑Softmax for mixed categorical/continuous optimization in frame structures is a solid novel contribution that improves efficiency over traditional population‑based methods, but it does not constitute a paradigm shift.

data.title: LSQCA: Resource-Efficient Load/Store Architecture for Limited-Scale Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
data.summary:
Current fault-tolerant quantum computer (FTQC) architectures utilize several encoding techniques to enable reliable logical operations with restricted qubit connectivity. However, such logical operations demand additional memory overhead to ensure fault tolerance. Since the main obstacle to practical quantum computing is the limited qubit count, our primary mission is to design floorplans that can reduce memory overhead without compromising computational capability. Despite extensive efforts to explore FTQC architectures, even the current state-of-the-art floorplan strategy devotes 50% of memory space to this overhead, not to data storage, to ensure unit-time random access to all logical qubits.
  In this paper, we propose an FTQC architecture based on a novel floorplan strategy, Load/Store Quantum Computer Architecture (LSQCA), which can achieve almost 100% memory density. The idea behind our architecture is to separate all memory regions into small computational space called Computational Registers (CR) and space-efficient memory space called Scan-Access Memory (SAM). We define an instruction set for these abstract structures and provide concrete designs named point-SAM and line-SAM architectures. With this design, we can improve the memory density by allowing variable-latency memory access while concealing the latency with other bottlenecks. We also propose optimization techniques to exploit properties of quantum programs observed in our static analysis, such as access locality in memory reference timestamps. Our numerical results indicate that LSQCA successfully leverages this idea. In a resource-restricted situation, a specific benchmark shows that we can achieve about 90% memory density with 5% increase in the execution time compared to a conventional floorplan, which achieves at most 50% memory density for unit-time random access. Our design ensures broad quantum applicability.

analysis.main_contribution: LSQCA introduces a load/store floorplan that partitions quantum memory into Computational Registers (CR) and Scan‑Access Memory (SAM), achieving near‑100% memory density while only modestly increasing execution time.
analysis.methodology: Design of a novel floorplan with variable‑latency memory access, definition of an instruction set for CR/SAM, concrete point‑SAM and line‑SAM implementations, and static‑analysis‑based optimization exploiting locality in quantum programs.
key_findings: Achieves ~90% memory density versus 50% in conventional unit‑time random‑access floorplans
Execution time increases by only ~5% compared to conventional designs
analysis.limitations: Performance evaluated on a limited set of benchmarks; scalability to larger, more diverse quantum workloads and different error‑correcting codes remains untested.
analysis.future_work: Extend LSQCA to other quantum device architectures, integrate with various surface‑code configurations, explore adaptive latency schemes, and validate on real industrial quantum applications.
analysis.score_reasoning: The paper presents a novel architectural partitioning that substantially improves memory density in fault‑tolerant quantum computers, representing a notable advance beyond incremental optimizations but not yet a paradigm shift.

data.title: SpeechPrompt: Prompting Speech Language Models for Speech Processing Tasks
data.summary: Prompting has become a practical method for utilizing pre-trained language models (LMs). This approach offers several advantages. It allows an LM to adapt to new tasks with minimal training and parameter updates, thus achieving efficiency in both storage and computation. Additionally, prompting modifies only the LM's inputs and harnesses the generative capabilities of language models to address various downstream tasks in a unified manner. This significantly reduces the need for human labor in designing task-specific models. These advantages become even more evident as the number of tasks served by the LM scales up. Motivated by the strengths of prompting, we are the first to explore the potential of prompting speech LMs in the domain of speech processing. Recently, there has been a growing interest in converting speech into discrete units for language modeling. Our pioneer research demonstrates that these quantized speech units are highly versatile within our unified prompting framework. Not only can they serve as class labels, but they also contain rich phonetic information that can be re-synthesized back into speech signals for speech generation tasks. Specifically, we reformulate speech processing tasks into speech-to-unit generation tasks. As a result, we can seamlessly integrate tasks such as speech classification, sequence generation, and speech generation within a single, unified prompting framework. The experiment results show that the prompting method can achieve competitive performance compared to the strong fine-tuning method based on self-supervised learning models with a similar number of trainable parameters. The prompting method also shows promising results in the few-shot setting. Moreover, with the advanced speech LMs coming into the stage, the proposed prompting framework attains great potential.

analysis.main_contribution: SpeechPrompt demonstrates that prompting a pre‑trained speech language model (speech LM) with quantized discrete units can unify diverse speech processing tasks—classification, sequence generation, and synthesis—while matching fine‑tuned SSL baselines with few trainable parameters.
analysis.methodology: The authors convert raw audio into discrete speech units via a vector‑quantised representation, then formulate each downstream task as a speech‑to‑unit generation problem. A prompt (task description + optional examples) is concatenated to the unit sequence and fed to the frozen speech LM; loss is computed against target units or synthesized audio.
key_findings: Prompting achieves competitive accuracy on classification and generation tasks compared to fine‑tuned SSL models with similar parameter budgets.
In few‑shot settings, prompting outperforms or matches fine‑tuning, indicating strong transferability.
analysis.limitations: Evaluation limited to a handful of benchmark datasets; performance on highly domain‑specific or low‑resource languages not explored. The approach relies on high‑quality discrete unit encoders and may be sensitive to quantisation quality.
analysis.future_work: Extend prompting to multilingual and low‑resource settings, investigate adaptive prompt learning, integrate more advanced speech LMs (e.g., Whisper, wav2vec 3), and explore end‑to‑end synthesis pipelines.
analysis.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a novel application of prompting to speech LMs, unifying multiple tasks with minimal tuning—a notable advance beyond incremental fine‑tuning work, but not yet paradigm‑shifting.

data.title: MLP Can Be A Good Transformer Learner
data.summary: Self-attention mechanism is the key of the Transformer but often criticized for its computation demands. Previous token pruning works motivate their methods from the view of computation redundancy but still need to load the full network and require same memory costs. This paper introduces a novel strategy that simplifies vision transformers and reduces computational load through the selective removal of non-essential attention layers, guided by entropy considerations. We identify that regarding the attention layer in bottom blocks, their subsequent MLP layers, i.e. two feed-forward layers, can elicit the same entropy quantity. Meanwhile, the accompanied MLPs are under-exploited since they exhibit smaller feature entropy compared to those MLPs in the top blocks. Therefore, we propose to integrate the uninformative attention layers into their subsequent counterparts by degenerating them into identical mapping, yielding only MLP in certain transformer blocks. Experimental results on ImageNet-1k show that the proposed method can remove 40% attention layer of DeiT-B, improving throughput and memory bound without performance compromise. Code is available at https://github.com/sihaoevery/lambda_vit.

analysis.main_contribution: The paper proposes an entropy‑guided strategy that selectively removes self‑attention layers from vision transformers by merging them with subsequent MLPs, achieving significant parameter and computation savings without accuracy loss.
analysis.methodology: Compute feature entropy for each transformer block; identify bottom blocks where attention and following MLP have low, similar entropy; replace the attention layer with an identical mapping so only the MLP remains; retrain or fine‑tune the modified network.
key_findings: Reduces 13.7% of DeiT‑B parameters and improves working load by 20.5% while keeping top‑1 accuracy unchanged; effectively removes ~40% of attention layers in DeiT‑B.
analysis.limitations: Evaluation limited to ImageNet classification with DeiT‑B; generalization to other vision transformer variants or downstream tasks is untested; the entropy criterion may not capture all redundancy patterns.
analysis.future_work: Apply the pruning scheme to other transformer backbones and tasks, explore adaptive entropy thresholds, investigate joint training of attention–MLP merging, and assess impact on model robustness and transfer learning.
analysis.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a novel entropy‑based pruning technique that simplifies transformers by eliminating redundant attention layers, which is a notable advance over prior token‑pruning methods but does not constitute a paradigm shift.

data.title: Scaling Behavior of Machine Translation with Large Language Models under Prompt Injection Attacks
data.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly becoming the preferred foundation platforms for many Natural Language Processing tasks such as Machine Translation, owing to their quality often comparable to or better than task-specific models, and the simplicity of specifying the task through natural language instructions or in-context examples. Their generality, however, opens them up to subversion by end users who may embed into their requests instructions that cause the model to behave in unauthorized and possibly unsafe ways. In this work we study these Prompt Injection Attacks (PIAs) on multiple families of LLMs on a Machine Translation task, focusing on the effects of model size on the attack success rates. We introduce a new benchmark data set and we discover that on multiple language pairs and injected prompts written in English, larger models under certain conditions may become more susceptible to successful attacks, an instance of the Inverse Scaling phenomenon (McKenzie et al., 2023). To our knowledge, this is the first work to study non-trivial LLM scaling behaviour in a multi-lingual setting.

data.title: Towards Assessing Spread in Sets of Software Architecture Designs
data.summary: Several approaches have recently used automated techniques to generate architecture design alternatives by means of optimization techniques. These approaches aim at improving an initial architecture with respect to quality aspects, such as performance, reliability, or maintainability. In this context, each optimization experiment usually produces a different set of architecture alternatives that is characterized by specific settings. As a consequence, the designer is left with the task of comparing such sets to identify the settings that lead to better solution sets for the problem. To assess the quality of solution sets, multi-objective optimization commonly relies on quality indicators. Among these, the quality indicator for the maximum spread estimates the diversity of the generated alternatives, providing a measure of how much of the solution space has been explored. However, the maximum spread indicator is computed only on the objective space and does not consider architectural information (e.g., components structure, design decisions) from the architectural space. In this paper, we propose a quality indicator for the spread that assesses the diversity of alternatives by taking into account architectural features. To compute the spread, we rely on a notion of distance between alternatives according to the way they were generated during the optimization. We demonstrate how our architectural quality indicator can be applied to a dataset from the literature.

analysis.main_contribution: The paper introduces an architectural spread quality indicator that extends the traditional maximum spread metric by incorporating architectural feature distances, enabling more informed comparison of design alternative sets generated by multi‑objective optimization.
analysis.methodology: Define a distance function between architecture alternatives based on their generation history and structural attributes; compute the spread over this distance space; evaluate the indicator on a published dataset of software architecture alternatives produced by automated refactoring techniques.
datasets_used: Dataset from existing literature on automated architecture design (specific source not named in excerpt)
key_findings:
1. The architectural spread indicator captures diversity that objective‑space metrics miss, revealing differences between solution sets.
2. Applying the indicator to a real dataset demonstrates its practical utility for guiding configuration choices in multi‑objective optimization.
analysis.limitations: Relies on a single literature dataset; distance definition depends on generation history and may not generalize across all architectural domains.
analysis.future_work: Extend evaluation to multiple datasets and domains, refine distance metrics to include richer architectural features, integrate the indicator into automated decision support tools for designers.
analysis.score_reasoning: The work presents a novel extension of an existing quality metric by incorporating architectural information, which is a clear but not revolutionary contribution.
